title: SDK Integration Walkthrough - Acme Retail
next_steps: Send Python and TypeScript SDK quickstart repos and example apps
Share SOC 2 and security pack + KMS integration notes
Provide pricing estimate for Dedicated capacity and burst options
action_items: Jordan Lee - Email quickstart repo links and high-level pricing - 2026-03-03
Priya Patel - Run a small latency/throughput benchmark using Acme's short prompt set and share results - 2026-03-06
Dana Chen - Share sample anonymized dataset and target latency SLOs - 2026-03-05
summary: AE + SE walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python & TypeScript). Covered auth via API key and env vars, quickstart commands, common integration patterns, console hints for keys and routes, and security/compliance Qs. Agreed next steps to run a short benchmark and start POC next week.
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan from Redwood Inference, and with me is priya our solutions engineer.
00:06 Priya Patel: hi all, excited to walk through the sdk quickstarts and get a sense of your env.
00:12 Dana Chen: thanks, we've been evaluating options for embedding and chat features, mainly focused on customer support summarization and search. timeframe is Q2 pilot.
00:26 Jordan Lee: perfect, can you remind us of your current stack? is it mostly node services and python batch jobs?
00:33 Marta Reyes: yeah node frontends, python workers for async tasks, some on-prem kubernetes for regulated flows. we care about data residency and key mgmt.
00:45 Priya Patel: got it — we'll show both python and typescript flows. first, auth is simple: api key via env var. examples: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx or set in your secrets manager.
00:58 Liam O'Connor: is there an sdk package or do we hit the rest api directly?
01:03 Priya Patel: we provide official sdks. python: pip install redwood-inference; ts: npm i @redwood/inference. both wrap the api and handle streaming.
01:15 Jordan Lee: and for private/vpc deployments you'll get a private endpoint and control plane for keys. for hosted you can manage api keys in the console.
01:24 Dana Chen: when you say console, is there a way to rotate keys and audit usage?
01:29 Priya Patel: yes — keys can be rotated in the console UI, and we surface token-level cost and latency breakdowns. audit logs are available for private customers and via the enterprise pack.
01:40 Jordan Lee: quick qual question — do you need SOC 2 and SSO for procurement?
01:44 Dana Chen: yes, SOC 2 required, SSO (okta) for engineers, and we prefer kms integration for encryption at rest.
01:52 Priya Patel: we support SOC 2, SAML/SSO, and KMS integrations for Private and Enterprise, and we can share the security pack after this call.
02:01 Jordan Lee: okay i'll add that to next steps. moving to a short demo — priya, can you show the python quickstart?
02:08 Priya Patel: sure. opening the repo now — apologies if transcription mangles code. python sample: from redwood import RedwoodClient client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get("REDWOOD_API_KEY")) resp = client.chat.create(model="redwood-alpha", messages=[{"role":"user","content":"summarize support ticket"}]) print(resp.text)
02:34 Liam O'Connor: are models pinned? how do we ensure stability in prod?
02:38 Priya Patel: yes — you can pin model versions in the api call or in the console route config. we also support rollout policies and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant if capacity is constrained.
02:51 Dana Chen: what about streaming tokens for live UX?
02:55 Priya Patel: streaming is supported in both sdks. ts snippet: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const stream = client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-alpha', messages: [...] }); stream.on('data', chunk => { /* append chunk */ });
03:12 Marta Reyes: ok, how does auth differ for private deployment? we have customer-managed k8s and a hardware hsm.
03:19 Priya Patel: for private you can integrate with your KMS/HSM and use short-lived keys issued by the control plane; networking is via VPC peering or private link.
03:28 Jordan Lee: cost question — high-level, what's the latency vs cost tradeoff we should expect for 7B vs 70B models?
03:35 Priya Patel: generally smaller models reduce token cost and latency; we recommend benchmark runs. our Optimize tool suggests quantization and batching configs. we can run a workload profile for your prompts and show unit economics.
03:48 Liam O'Connor: can the sdk handle batching on the client side or is that runtime?
03:53 Priya Patel: runtime handles continuous batching and kv cache. the sdks mostly handle request orchestration. we expose hints for batching and advise on best-effort client-side batching for very high throughput.
04:06 Jordan Lee: i'm going to share a sample benchmark plan — priya will run it against a small sample set. dana, if you can share the sample prompts that would be great.
04:14 Dana Chen: yes we'll share.
04:17 Priya Patel: switching to console quick look — in the routes tab you can create a route, pin a model, set a timeout, and attach an autoscaling policy. here's the keys area where you generate api keys and set scopes.
04:31 Marta Reyes: do you provide role-based access control? we need granular permissions for dev vs ops.
04:36 Priya Patel: yes rbac is available for enterprise customers; you can scope keys per-route, per-environment.
04:43 Liam O'Connor: for testing we'll probably start on hosted and then move to private if we need on-prem KMS.
04:50 Jordan Lee: that's a common pattern — hosted for quick pilot, then dedicated or private for compliance.
04:55 Dana Chen: any known limitations on request size or token limits?
04:59 Priya Patel: default seq length depends on model; we document token limits in the model catalog. very long contexts may need chunking or embeddings + rerank.
05:08 Jordan Lee: demo aside, procurement questions — what does the contract look like for dedicated?
05:12 Priya Patel: dedicated is a reserved capacity contract with monthly or annual commits, SLA-backed uptime, and support tiers. we can share a template.
05:21 Dana Chen: ok. one more — we use internal logging pipelines, can we forward audit logs?
05:25 Priya Patel: yes logs can be forwarded to your logging endpoints for Private and Dedicated with configurable retention.
05:33 Jordan Lee: let's run through a quick integration checklist for your engs.
05:37 Priya Patel: checklist: 1) create api key in console or control plane; 2) set REDWOOD_API_KEY in secrets manager; 3) pip/npm install sdk; 4) run quickstart sample; 5) add route and pin model in console; 6) run small benchmark and adjust batching/quantization per Optimize recommendations.
06:00 Liam O'Connor: can you share the quickstart link and a sample app?
06:04 Jordan Lee: we'll email repos — python quickstart, ts quickstart, and a tiny express app showing streaming.
06:11 Dana Chen: what about observability — per-route latency breakdown you mentioned?
06:15 Priya Patel: yes per-route dashboards in Console, token-level costing, tracing hooks and error analysis; you can also export traces to your APM.
06:25 Marta Reyes: security again — we need the SOC2 attestation before legal will sign.
06:29 Jordan Lee: noted, we'll attach the SOC2 report and security pack.
06:33 Dana Chen: ok great. final questions from my side: rolling upgrades and regression detection?
06:39 Priya Patel: we have rollout features — canary, A/B, automatic fallback, and Redwood Optimize can flag quality regressions tied to eval prompt sets.
06:50 Jordan Lee: thanks everyone. recap: jordan to send quickstarts and security pack; priya to run benchmark; acme to provide sample prompts and SLOs; schedule poc kick-off 3/9.
07:05 Dana Chen: thanks, talk soon.
07:07 Jordan Lee: thanks all, bye.
07:10 (call ends)
